cancho.title: A leaked file, refused by name

steps.note: It opens a file and never closes it. The compiler refuses:
steps.cmd: cancho check leak.cho --std

steps.note: The refusal is data an agent can match on:
steps.cmd: cancho check leak.cho --std --output json | grep '"rule"'

steps.note: One added line fixes it, and the program may now run:
steps.cmd: diff leak.cho fixed.cho; cancho build fixed.cho --std -o notes && ./notes

steps.note: What may it do? The types say:
steps.cmd: cancho authority fixed.cho --std
steps.out:
performs
    fs_read("/tmp")
    io_write
never touches
    the network
    the heap
    the command line
    signals
    other programs
    foreign code

cancho-ui.title: A component that asks for the clock

steps.note: Delete `requires Clock;` and the compiler refuses:
steps.cmd: cancho-ui check clock_bad.cui; echo "exit $?"
steps.out:
error[capability-missing] at clock_bad.cui:15:21: component `Clock` performs `clock.now` which requires the `Clock` capability, but `requires Clock` is not declared
exit 1

steps.note: With the declaration it is accepted:
steps.cmd: cancho-ui check clock.cui; echo "exit $?"

steps.note: Ask what it may reach, as data:
steps.cmd: cancho-ui inspect effects clock.cui Clock | grep '"capability"'

trail:shop-energy.title: A shop's energy, passed between roles
trail:shop-energy.summary: A data scientist, a statistician and a data engineer pass one file between them, each with their own command line, and cancho-tools to read what they print. No glue, no new package: a tool that dislikes the file says why, by rule.
trail:shop-energy.source: A recorded run of the real tools, replayed, on synthetic data (examples/shop-energy/make_data.py): nothing here measures a real shop.

steps.note: Data scientist (ml): I take the file as it came. The tool refuses, and names the row and the rule.
steps.cmd: ml fit --model linear --target kwh --output kwh.ml shop.csv > refusal.json; jsonq -p /error/rule --format text refusal.json; jsonq -p /error/detail --format text refusal.json

steps.note: Statistician (stats): What is wrong with it? Three cells are missing in the target.
steps.cmd: stats describe shop.csv --cols kwh > kwh.json; for k in count missing mean; do echo "$k $(jsonq -p /data/columns/0/$k --format text kwh.json)"; done

steps.note: Data engineer (table): I drop the rows with no reading, and hand the rest on. peek counts the lines: the header and 117 rows.
steps.cmd: table --where "kwh != ''" --format csv shop.csv > clean.csv; peek --count-lines --lines 1:1 clean.csv | jsonq -p /data/total_lines --format text -

steps.note: Statistician (stats): Same question on the clean file: exact figures, with the median.
steps.cmd: stats describe clean.csv --cols kwh > clean.json; for k in count missing mean sd quantiles/2/value; do echo "$k $(jsonq -p /data/columns/0/$k --format text clean.json)"; done

chart.title: kwh, the 117 clean readings: stats' exact histogram

steps.note: Data engineer (table): The readings are in time order, so I hold out the last 24 rows and hand over the 93 before them. peek counts lines, the header included.
steps.cmd: table --select hour,outside_c,open,kwh --limit 93 --format csv clean.csv > train.csv; table --select hour,outside_c,open,kwh --from 93 --format csv clean.csv > test.csv; for f in train test; do echo "$f $(peek --count-lines --lines 1:1 $f.csv | jsonq -p /data/total_lines --format text -) lines"; done

steps.note: Data scientist (ml): I fit on the 93 earlier rows and score on the 24 the model never saw.
steps.cmd: ml fit --model linear --target kwh --output kwh.ml train.csv > fit.json; ml eval --model-file kwh.ml test.csv > eval.json; ml predict --model-file kwh.ml test.csv > pred.json; for m in rmse mae r2; do echo "$m $(jsonq -p /data/metrics/$m --format text eval.json)"; done

chart.title: The 24 held-out rows: predicted against actual

steps.note: Reviewer (jsonq, peek): Before this ships: what may each tool do, the reading tools included? The compilers proved it.
steps.cmd: for t in table stats ml jsonq peek; do echo "$t $($t introspect | jsonq -p /authority/effects --format text -)"; done

trail:late-parcels.title: A parcel-lateness service: data, model, deploy, drift, retrain
trail:late-parcels.summary: Data and a model before deploy; the service's own traffic and next month's parcels after. Every step is a real run of a cancho tool, and the seam where cancho-client-gen refuses ml-serve's OpenAPI document is shown as it is.
trail:late-parcels.source: A recorded run of the real tools, replayed, on synthetic data (examples/late-parcels/make_data.py): nothing here measures a real courier.

steps.note: Data engineer: 400 parcels from last month. Three scanner dropouts have no distance; I drop them. peek counts the lines, header included.
steps.cmd: table --where "distance_km != ''" --format csv parcels.csv > clean.csv; peek --count-lines --lines 1:1 clean.csv | jsonq -p /data/total_lines --format text -

steps.note: Statistician: how far do parcels travel, and how many are late? (late is 0 or 1, so its mean is the late share)
steps.cmd: stats describe clean.csv --cols distance_km,late > desc.json; echo "distance_km mean $(jsonq -p /data/columns/0/mean --format text desc.json)"; echo "late share $(jsonq -p /data/columns/1/mean --format text desc.json)"

chart.title: Distance of last month's 397 parcels (stats' exact histogram)

steps.note: Data scientist: a logistic model for lateness, scored on the fifth of the rows ml holds out.
steps.cmd: ml fit --model logistic --target late --split train=0.8 --seed 1 --output late.ml clean.csv > fit.json; for m in accuracy recall roc_auc; do echo "$m $(jsonq -p /data/summary/holdout/metrics/$m --format text fit.json)"; done

steps.note: Deploy: serve the model. It answers on loopback, and /health says which model file it holds, by SHA-256.
steps.cmd:
ml-serve --model-file late.ml --port 18900 2> serve.log &
curl -s localhost:18900/health | jsonq -p /model_sha256 --format text -

steps.note: Asking it to listen on every address is refused unless a token file guards it.
steps.cmd: ml-serve --model-file late.ml --bind all 2>&1 | jsonq -p /error/rule --format text -

steps.note: A parcel (42 km, 5 pm, raining) is predicted late. A distance written as text is refused, and the refusal points at the field.
steps.cmd:
curl -s -XPOST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"distance_km":42.5,"hour":17,"rain":1}' localhost:18900/predict | jsonq -p /rows/0 --format text -
curl -s -XPOST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"distance_km":"far","hour":9,"rain":0}' localhost:18900/predict > bad.json; jsonq -p /rule --format text bad.json; jsonq -p /errors/0 --format text bad.json

steps.note: Frontend: I want a typed client from the server's own OpenAPI document. The generator refuses it.
steps.cmd: curl -s localhost:18900/openapi.json > openapi.json; clientgen openapi.json --python -o client.py; echo "exit $?"
steps.out:
clientgen: openapi.json: a schema is of no kind the model names
exit 1

steps.note: What did the server log? A line per request, never a payload. Three more calls, then count the statuses.
steps.cmd: for i in 1 2 3; do curl -s -XPOST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"distance_km":10,"hour":9,"rain":0}' localhost:18900/predict > /dev/null; done; tail -n +2 serve.log | tally --field 3 --delim ' ' | jsonq -p /data/top --format text -

steps.note: A month later. The rainy season: the parcels are not the ones the model learned from.
steps.cmd: for f in clean next; do stats describe $f.csv --cols distance_km,rain > $f.json; echo "$f: distance_km mean $(jsonq -p /data/columns/0/mean --format text $f.json), rain share $(jsonq -p /data/columns/1/mean --format text $f.json)"; done
steps.out:
clean: distance_km mean 25.157178841309825, rain share 0.33753148614609574
next: distance_km mean 36.12166666666667, rain share 0.6

chart.title: Share of parcels delivered in the rain
chart.short: Share of parcels in the rain

steps.note: The labels for the new month have come in. Score the model on all 300 new parcels.
steps.cmd: ml eval --model-file late.ml next.csv > next_eval.json; for m in accuracy recall; do echo "$m $(jsonq -p /data/metrics/$m --format text next_eval.json)"; done

steps.note: Retrain on last month plus the first 200 new parcels, and keep the last 100 aside to judge it.
steps.cmd: S=distance_km,hour,rain,late; table --select $S --limit 200 --format csv next.csv > next_train.csv; table --select $S --from 200 --format csv next.csv > next_test.csv; (cat clean.csv; tail -n +2 next_train.csv) > both.csv; for f in both next_test; do echo "$f $(peek --count-lines --lines 1:1 $f.csv | jsonq -p /data/total_lines --format text -) lines"; done

steps.note: Same 100 parcels, old model against the retrained one.
steps.cmd: ml fit --model logistic --target late --output late2.ml both.csv > fit2.json; for m in late late2; do ml eval --model-file $m.ml next_test.csv > $m.json; echo "$m accuracy $(jsonq -p /data/metrics/accuracy --format text $m.json) recall $(jsonq -p /data/metrics/recall --format text $m.json)"; done
steps.out:
late accuracy "0.83" recall "0.782608695652174"
late2 accuracy "0.89" recall "0.855072463768116"

chart.title: Accuracy: the old model against the retrained one

steps.note: Redeploy. A reload is a restart, and /health shows the model file changed.
steps.cmd:
ml-serve --model-file late2.ml --port 18900 2>> serve.log &
curl -s localhost:18900/health | jsonq -p /model_sha256 --format text -

steps.note: Reviewer: what may each tool do? The compilers proved it.
steps.cmd: for t in ml-serve ml table stats; do echo "$t $($t introspect | jsonq -p /authority/effects --format text -)"; done

trail:model-review.title: Trust a model change you didn't write
trail:model-review.summary: A teammate's agent retrains a model and claims a big gain. A reviewer who never reads the training code checks the claim with run records, a join on customer ids, a clean holdout and a guarded write.
trail:model-review.source: A recorded run of the real tools, replayed, on synthetic data (examples/model-review/make_data.py): nothing here measures a real service.

steps.note: Reviewer: before judging a model, is the frozen holdout like the data it will be judged against? Compare the churn rate and tenure.
steps.cmd: for f in train holdout; do stats describe $f.csv --cols tenure_months,churned > $f.json; echo "$f: churn rate $(jsonq -p /data/columns/1/mean --format text $f.json), mean tenure $(jsonq -p /data/columns/0/mean --format text $f.json)"; done
steps.out:
train: churn rate 0.59, mean tenure 30.5
holdout: churn rate 0.53, mean tenure 30.5

steps.note: Teammate's agent: the model in production uses tenure only. I trained a forest on every feature, and tracked both runs. (The PR's claim: accuracy 0.977 against 0.758.)
steps.cmd: ml fit --model logistic --target churned --drop id,monthly_spend,tickets_90d --track runs --output prod/model.ml train.csv > /dev/null; ml fit --model forest --task classification --target churned --drop id --track runs --output cand.ml candidate_train.csv > /dev/null; ml runs list runs > runs.json; echo "$(ls runs | wc -l) run records"

steps.note: Reviewer: what do the run records say about each run?
steps.cmd: for i in 0 1; do echo "$(jsonq -p /data/runs/$i/model --format text runs.json) trained on $(jsonq -p /data/runs/$i/train_rows --format text runs.json) rows, scored on $(jsonq -p /data/runs/$i/metrics_on --format text runs.json)"; done
steps.out:
"logistic" trained on 400 rows, scored on "train"
"forest" trained on 480 rows, scored on "train"

steps.note: Compare them: the inputs that differ, and the headline numbers. The new model had 80 more training rows, and the 0.977 is a score on training data.
steps.cmd: A=$(jsonq -p /data/runs/0/id --format text runs.json | tr -d '"'); B=$(jsonq -p /data/runs/1/id --format text runs.json | tr -d '"'); ml runs compare runs $A $B > cmp.json; echo "training rows $(jsonq -p /data/inputs/3/a --format text cmp.json) -> $(jsonq -p /data/inputs/3/b --format text cmp.json)"; echo "accuracy $(jsonq -p /data/metrics/0/a --format text cmp.json) -> $(jsonq -p /data/metrics/0/b --format text cmp.json)"

steps.note: Where did the 80 extra rows come from? A join on customer id: how many of the candidate's training customers are in the frozen holdout?
steps.cmd: table --query "select count(*) as overlap from 'candidate_train.csv' as a inner join 'holdout.csv' as b on a.id = b.id" | jsonq -p /data/rows/0/0 --format text -

steps.note: So 80 of the 200 holdout customers were trained on. An anti join leaves the customers neither model has seen.
steps.cmd: table --query "select b.id, b.tenure_months, b.monthly_spend, b.tickets_90d, b.churned from 'holdout.csv' as b anti join 'candidate_train.csv' as a on b.id = a.id" --format csv > clean_holdout.csv; peek --count-lines --lines 1:1 clean_holdout.csv | jsonq -p /data/total_lines --format text -

steps.note: Score on customers it never saw. The honest gain is smaller than the claim, but it is real.
steps.cmd: echo "production, clean holdout            $(ml eval --model-file prod/model.ml clean_holdout.csv --drop id,monthly_spend,tickets_90d | jsonq -p /data/metrics/accuracy --format text -)"; echo "candidate, full holdout (leaked)     $(ml eval --model-file cand.ml holdout.csv --drop id | jsonq -p /data/metrics/accuracy --format text -)"; echo "candidate, clean holdout             $(ml eval --model-file cand.ml clean_holdout.csv --drop id | jsonq -p /data/metrics/accuracy --format text -)"
steps.out:
production, clean holdout            "0.725"
candidate, full holdout (leaked)     "0.895"
candidate, clean holdout             "0.85"

chart.title: Accuracy: the claim against what the review found

steps.note: Teammate's agent: retrained on the training file only, tracked. Reviewer: the run record can be replayed, and the clean holdout is the test.
steps.cmd: ml fit --model forest --task classification --target churned --drop id --track runs --output cand2.ml train.csv > fit3.json; R=$(jsonq -p /data/run/id --format text fit3.json | tr -d '"'); echo "replay verifies: $(ml runs verify runs $R | jsonq -p /data/verified --format text -)"; echo "clean holdout accuracy $(ml eval --model-file cand2.ml clean_holdout.csv --drop id | jsonq -p /data/metrics/accuracy --format text -)"
steps.out:
replay verifies: true
clean holdout accuracy "0.8666666666666667"

steps.note: Promote it, guarded: the write only happens if production still holds the file the reviewer looked at.
steps.cmd: H=$(env hash --root prod model.ml --format text | cut -d' ' -f1); write --root prod --if-sha256 $H --stdin model.ml < cand2.ml > promote.json; echo "promoted: $(jsonq -p /data/changed --format text promote.json), now $(jsonq -p /data/after_sha256 --format text promote.json)"; echo $H > old_hash.txt

steps.note: Another agent, which read production before this promotion, tries to promote the original, leaked candidate. The write is refused, and says what the file holds now.
steps.cmd: write --root prod --if-sha256 $(cat old_hash.txt) --stdin model.ml < cand.ml > stale.json; jsonq -p /error/rule --format text stale.json; jsonq -p /error/detail/actual_sha256 --format text stale.json

steps.note: Reviewer: what may each tool do? The compilers proved it, and none of them reaches the network.
steps.cmd: for t in ml table stats write hash; do echo "$t $(env $t introspect | jsonq -p /authority/effects --format text -)"; done

trail:ship-an-api.title: Ship an API: declare, generate a client, use it, change it, package it
trail:ship-an-api.summary: One declaration is the service, its OpenAPI document and the source of a typed client. An app uses it, the data it generates is analysed, an agent changes the contract, and the service is packaged as a reproducible image. Every step is a real run of a cancho tool; the seams that do not meet are shown as they are.
trail:ship-an-api.source: A recorded run of the real tools, replayed, on synthetic users (examples/ship-an-api/app.py): nothing here measures a real service. cancho-web's own users example is the service.

steps.note: Build the service from its one declaration (routes, bodies, errors), and start it. The compiler is the revision cancho-web pins.
steps.cmd: (cd cancho-web && scripts/build.sh examples/users/users.cho ../users-v1); ./users-v1 18950 2> serve.log &  curl -s localhost:18950/health

steps.note: A bad request is refused with every error at once, each with its JSON Pointer, as problem+json.
steps.cmd: curl -s -XPOST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"","age":151}' localhost:18950/users > refusal.json; for p in /count /errors/0 /errors/1; do jsonq -p $p --format text refusal.json; done

steps.note: The OpenAPI 3.1 document comes from the same declaration, so a route cannot be served and undocumented.
steps.cmd: curl -s localhost:18950/openapi.json > openapi.json; jsonq -p /paths --keys --format text openapi.json

steps.note: Frontend: a typed client from the server's own document. clientgen reads it, lists what it found, and writes Python.
steps.cmd: clientgen openapi.json --check; clientgen openapi.json --model | head -3; clientgen openapi.json --python -o client.py
steps.out:
ok 5 operations, 4 components
get /health -> health (0 parameters, body none, 1 responses: 200=object )
get /users -> listUsers (2 parameters, body none, 2 responses: 200=Page 422=Problem )
post /users -> createUser (0 parameters, body NewUser, 5 responses: 201=User 400=Problem 415=Problem 422=Problem 503=Problem )

steps.note: The client's annotations promise a dataclass. Does it return one? (A read-only call, so the service stays empty. An earlier build of clientgen returned a plain dict here; that is fixed in cancho-client-gen#15.)
steps.cmd: seek --format text 'def listUsers' client.py; python3 -c "import client; r = client.Client('http://127.0.0.1:18950').listUsers(limit=1); print(type(r).__name__, r)"
steps.out:
client.py:79:    def listUsers(self, *, limit: int | None = None, offset: int | None = None) -> Page:
Page Page(total=0, items=[])

steps.note: The app (a stand-in for whatever uses the service) registers 200 users through the client. Some are invalid on purpose.
steps.cmd: python3 app.py http://127.0.0.1:18950

steps.note: What did the launch traffic get back, and which fields were refused?
steps.cmd: table --group status --agg count --sort status --format csv requests.csv; table --where "status = 422" --group field --agg count --sort -count --format csv requests.csv

steps.note: What does the service hold now? Ages of the registered users, and how many are over 120. (table compares text unless a column says :int.)
steps.cmd: stats describe users.csv --cols age > ages.json; for k in count mean max; do echo "$k $(jsonq -p /data/columns/0/$k --format text ages.json)"; done; echo "older than 120: $(table --where 'age:int > 120' --agg count --format csv users.csv | tail -1)"

chart.title: Ages of the users the service holds (stats' exact histogram)

steps.note: An agent proposes a tighter limit: no age above 120. replace edits the one line of the declaration, and refuses unless it matches exactly once.
steps.cmd: replace --root cancho-web --old 'schema.new_int(heap, s2, 0, 150)' --new 'schema.new_int(heap, s2, 0, 120)' --expect 1 examples/users/users.cho | jsonq -p /data/replacements --format text -

steps.note: Rebuild it as a static executable (the linker wrapper adds -static) and restart. The served document now says 120.
steps.cmd: (cd cancho-web && CC=static-cc scripts/build.sh examples/users/users.cho ../users-v2); ./users-v2 18950 2> serve.log &  curl -s localhost:18950/openapi.json > openapi2.json; for f in openapi openapi2; do echo "$f: max age $(jsonq -p /components/schemas/NewUser/properties/age/maximum --format text $f.json)"; done
steps.out:
openapi: max age 150
openapi2: max age 120

steps.note: Does the client need regenerating? The limit lives in the server's schema.
steps.cmd: clientgen openapi2.json --python -o client2.py; diff client.py client2.py > /dev/null && echo 'client unchanged'

steps.note: A 130-year-old customer, who was valid yesterday.
steps.cmd: curl -s -XPOST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Old","age":130}' localhost:18950/users > old.json; jsonq -p /errors/0 --format text old.json

steps.note: Package it. A dynamically linked program is refused by rule; the static one becomes an image, built twice into two directories: the same binary gives the same image. (Two builds of the source differ by 2 bytes, so a fresh build has a new digest.)
steps.cmd: mkdir -p root img0/blobs/sha256 img/blobs/sha256 img2/blobs/sha256; cp users-v1 root/users; oci-build --root root --out img0 --platform linux/amd64 --bin users:app/users; cp users-v2 root/users; oci-build --root root --out img --platform linux/amd64 --bin users:app/users; oci-build --root root --out img2 --platform linux/amd64 --bin users:app/users; diff -r img img2 && echo 'the two images are identical'
steps.out:
refused: elf-dynamic (app/users)
sha256:b7a58f0d56b285d248bc8781fa69f0e66ea7096e4bb1e64e7a8610c03da290fa
sha256:b7a58f0d56b285d248bc8781fa69f0e66ea7096e4bb1e64e7a8610c03da290fa
the two images are identical

steps.note: What may the service do? The compiler proved it.
steps.cmd: (cd cancho-web && cancho authority examples/users/users.cho src/*.cho build/deps/*.cho --std | awk '/provably pure/{exit}{print}' | tr -s ' \n' ' ')
steps.out: performs args clock conn_accept conn_read conn_write err_write heap net_in("") poll never touches the filesystem signals other programs foreign code
